items.title: Clay Jenkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 18, 2016
items.q: Like Rufus Reid, when he’s playing, he’s in charge of the rhythm section you know?

ctx.x: Interesting question. Because a lot of my very very best friends are bass players. Yeah because I really love bass. One of my best friends, Jeff Campbell at the Eastman School is beautiful bass player. But I’ve known guys, well John Clayton is a great bass player and he’s one of my heroes and a guy named Bob Bowman in Kansas City a guy that I was on Buddy’s band with, Tom Warrington, and a friend of mine in school named

George Anderson — all these guys were bass players. So I guess just a big beat and someone you can really trust in terms of the time and the form. Because there’s so much, especially in more modern music there’s so much responsibility to a bass player. Because he’s really in charge — to me he’s in charge of the beat and he’s in charge of the harmony, which means he’s in charge of the form. Like Rufus Reid, when he’s playing, he’s in charge of the rhythm section you know? So he wouldn’t say that, but he is. So…

Very interesting. Like most musicians, I’m guessing you have a list, under all instruments you have your list. I’m going to say this question from a backwards standpoint. What gets people less likely to be called by you? What makes a musician sort of move down your list as far as filling a gig?
